notes:
Task and constraints: Find the smallest number that appears on neither side of any card after optionally flipping cards.
Idea: Exclude every number that appears equal on the front and back of the same card, then take the minimum remaining visible candidate.
Technique and why it applies: A number identical on both sides can never be hidden by flipping that card. Any other number can be placed on the back side of its card, so the smallest such value is the answer.
Invariant: The exclusion set contains all values that cannot be hidden because they appear on both sides of a card.
Edge cases: If every value is excluded, the fallback returns zero as required. The code constructs the set repeatedly in the list comprehension, which is wasteful but preserves the result.
Complexity: Set construction is repeated for each candidate, giving O(n²) time in the worst case and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the smallest number that can be visible on one side of a card without being forced to appear on both sides.
Idea: Build the set of values on cards whose front and back are equal, then scan all front and back values for the smallest allowed candidate.
Technique and why it applies: Equal-side values are impossible to hide; every other value can be made the visible side by flipping its card.
Invariant: same contains the values forbidden from being the final visible number.
Edge cases: If no candidate survives, infinity is retained and the function returns zero. The code assumes fronts and backs have equal lengths.
Complexity: The scans are O(n) expected time and O(n) space for the exclusion set.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees whose nodes are values from arr and whose parent equals the product of its two children, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Memoize the number of trees rooted at each value by enumerating factor pairs present in the input set.
Technique and why it applies: Each root contributes one single-node tree. Every valid pair of child values contributes helper(left)*helper(right) possible left/right subtrees.
Invariant: helper(num) stores the number of valid trees rooted at num.
Edge cases: lru_cache is used but not imported in the snippet. The set iteration includes both (a,b) and (b,a), which correctly counts ordered left/right child arrangements; the code assumes positive factors.
Complexity: With n distinct values, memoized states scan all n factors, giving O(n²) time and O(n) memo space, aside from big-integer costs.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees where each non-leaf parent is the product of its two child values.
Idea: Sort values and compute the number of trees rooted at each value using previously computed factor values.
Technique and why it applies: For each smaller A[j] dividing A[i], the quotient must already be in dp; their tree counts multiply to form valid ordered children. dp starts at one for the single-node tree.
Invariant: dp[x] is the number of valid trees with root value x, modulo 10^9+7.
Edge cases: A is sorted in place. The factor pair is counted in ordered orientations because the loop visits each possible left factor.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), the nested pair scan is O(n²), and the map uses O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Convert each word in a sentence to Goat Latin while preserving word order and adding a growing suffix.
Idea: For each word, keep it if it begins with a vowel; otherwise move its first character to the end, then append ma and an increasing run of a's.
Technique and why it applies: index records the word's one-based position, determining the number of trailing a characters.
Invariant: result contains the converted words processed so far, separated by single spaces.
Edge cases: sentence.split(' ') preserves empty entries caused by repeated spaces, which can create indexing errors for empty words. Standard input is expected to have single spaces between nonempty words.
Complexity: Conversion takes O(total output length) time and space, though repeated string concatenation may add copying overhead.

Task and constraints: Convert a sentence to Goat Latin by applying the word rule and appending ma plus a position-dependent suffix.
Idea: Split on whitespace and lazily yield each converted word.
Technique and why it applies: A word starting with a vowel stays in place; otherwise its first letter moves to the end. The suffix contains ma and i copies of a for the one-based word index i.
Invariant: Each yielded word is the correct Goat Latin transformation of the corresponding input word.
Edge cases: split() collapses repeated spaces and ignores leading/trailing whitespace, unlike splitting on a literal space. Empty input returns an empty string.
Complexity: The scan is O(total input and output characters) time and O(output length) space.

Task and constraints: Count directed friend requests under the age eligibility rules.
Idea: Count each age and sum eligible ordered sender-recipient pairs by age groups.
Technique and why it applies: request implements the age condition; multiplying c[a] by c[b] counts all pairs, then subtracting one when ages match excludes self-requests for each sender.
Invariant: c[a] and c[b] are the frequencies of the two age groups being considered.
Edge cases: The rule rejects requests from younger senders to older recipients and accounts for the same-age group without self-pairs. The code assumes ages are valid inputs.
Complexity: Counter construction is O(n), then every distinct age pair is checked, taking O(U²) time and O(U) space for U distinct ages.

Task and constraints: Maximize total job profit by assigning each worker at most one job no harder than their ability.
Idea: Sort jobs by difficulty, build prefix maximum profits, and binary-search the hardest feasible job for each worker.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix maxima ensure the selected profit is best among all jobs no harder than the worker's ability. Binary search finds the rightmost feasible difficulty.
Invariant: arr[j][1] stores the maximum profit among jobs up to index j in difficulty order.
Edge cases: The snippet uses inf without importing or defining it, so it fails unless that name exists externally. A worker with no feasible job earns zero.
Complexity: Sorting jobs costs O(n log n), prefix maxima O(n), and workers' searches O(m log n), for O(n log n+m log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Maximize the island area obtainable by changing at most one water cell to land.
Idea: Union adjacent land cells into connected components, then evaluate each water cell by summing the sizes of its unique neighboring components plus one.
Technique and why it applies: DSU roots identify connected islands and rank[root] is used as component size. A set prevents counting the same island twice when it touches multiple sides of the water cell.
Invariant: Each land component's root stores its area in rank, and parent maps cells to their component root.
Edge cases: The cell ID uses i*m+j rather than i*n+j; this is correct only for square grids, which the original problem guarantees. An all-land grid is handled by the initial max rank.
Complexity: DSU processing and water-cell checks take near O(mn α(mn)) time and O(mn) space.

Task and constraints: Find the largest island size possible after changing at most one zero to one.
Idea: Flood-fill each existing island with a unique label and record its area, then test every zero by adding the areas of adjacent distinct islands.
Technique and why it applies: Relabeling cells avoids revisiting islands; a set deduplicates labels around a candidate zero so one island is not counted multiple times.
Invariant: area maps each island label to its size, and grid cells greater than one carry their island label.
Edge cases: If there is no land, result starts at zero and any zero can create an island of size one. The DFS is recursive and may hit recursion limits on very large grids.
Complexity: Each cell is visited a constant number of times, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) space.

Task and constraints: Sum the number of substrings in which each character appears exactly once.
Idea: For each character occurrence, count the substrings where that occurrence is the unique instance of its character.
Technique and why it applies: The distance to the previous occurrence determines left extension choices, and the distance to the next occurrence determines right extension choices. Their product counts substrings attributed to that occurrence.
Invariant: idx_recorder[c] lists all occurrence indices for character c in increasing order.
Edge cases: collections is used without an import in the snippet. The helper's local ans shadows the outer variable but returns its own correct per-character contribution.
Complexity: Recording indices and summing occurrence contributions take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Compute the total count of unique characters across every substring, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Attribute each substring's contribution to each character occurrence using its previous two occurrence positions.
Technique and why it applies: For an occurrence at i, (i-j)*(j-k) counts substrings where it is the only occurrence of that character, with -1 sentinels for the first two positions. A final pass accounts for occurrences after the string ends.
Invariant: index[c] stores the previous two positions of each uppercase letter.
Edge cases: The code assumes S contains only uppercase English letters because it indexes a fixed alphabet dictionary. The modulus is applied after every contribution.
Complexity: One scan plus a fixed 26-character final pass gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count the ways to express positive integer n as a sum of consecutive positive integers.
Idea: Increase the length i of a candidate sequence and maintain the offset sum of 0 through i-1.
Technique and why it applies: A sequence of length i starting at x sums to i*x + i(i-1)/2. Thus n is representable at that length when n-csum is divisible by i.
Invariant: csum equals the sum of the first i-1 nonnegative offsets for the current candidate length i.
Edge cases: The loop stops once csum reaches n, since longer sequences cannot start at a positive integer and sum to n. n is assumed positive.
Complexity: The loop runs O(sqrt(n)) iterations in practice due to the early break, with O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Return the start and end indices of every group of at least three identical consecutive characters.
Idea: Track the current run length and close a group when the character changes or the string ends.
Technique and why it applies: On a change, the previous run spans i-c through i-1. The final-run condition appends a group if the repeated character reaches the last index.
Invariant: c is the current run length and prev is its character.
Edge cases: The code uses bitwise & rather than logical and in the last-index condition; both operands are booleans here, so it still evaluates correctly. Empty input returns an empty list.
Complexity: Each character is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond results.

Task and constraints: Find every contiguous group of at least three equal characters and return its inclusive endpoints.
Idea: Track the beginning of each run and check its length when the run ends.
Technique and why it applies: A run ends when the current character is the last character or differs from the next character. Its length is j-i+1, so qualifying intervals are appended.
Invariant: i marks the beginning of the current run.
Edge cases: Empty strings return an empty list because the loop does not run. Indices are zero-based and inclusive.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond output.

Task and constraints: Mask an email address or phone number according to the personal-information formatting rules.
Idea: Branch on whether the input contains @; mask the email's local name or strip phone punctuation and preserve only the required trailing digits.
Technique and why it applies: Email masking keeps the first and last local characters and lowercases the domain pieces. Phone masking scans digits from right to left, replacing earlier digits and adding country-code markers based on the count.
Invariant: res is built as the masked output, while l tracks processed phone digits and flag indicates the prefix should be hidden.
Edge cases: The email branch assumes exactly one @ and a domain with exactly two dot-separated parts. Phone logic relies on string length as a proxy for processed digits and may mishandle some lengths.
Complexity: Each input character is scanned a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Flip each row horizontally and invert every binary pixel.
Idea: Reverse each row and replace each bit b with 1-b.
Technique and why it applies: Horizontal reversal changes the pixel order, and inversion swaps zero and one. The nested comprehension builds a new image.
Invariant: Each output row is the inverted reverse of its corresponding input row.
Edge cases: Empty images and empty rows yield corresponding empty lists. The input is not mutated.
Complexity: Every pixel is processed once, so time is O(RC) and output space is O(RC).

Task and constraints: Flip a binary image horizontally and invert its bits in place.
Idea: Swap symmetric entries in each row while XOR-inverting both values.
Technique and why it applies: For binary values, x^1 flips the bit. Pairing left index i with ~i, which is -i-1, swaps mirrored positions and inverts them in one operation.
Invariant: After each iteration, the outermost processed symmetric pair is in its final flipped-and-inverted state.
Edge cases: The middle element of an odd-length row is paired with itself and is inverted once by the tuple assignment. The input is mutated and returned.
Complexity: Each row takes O(C) time and O(1) auxiliary space; overall time is O(RC).

Task and constraints: Apply multiple source-to-target replacements to a string, only when each source matches at its specified original index.
Idea: Sort replacements by original index and apply them from left to right while tracking how earlier replacements shift later positions.
Technique and why it applies: offset adjusts each original index by the total length changes already applied. A replacement is performed only if the current slice equals its source.
Invariant: offset equals the cumulative length difference from successful replacements before the current original index.
Edge cases: The code prints debug messages on failed matches. If replacements have the same index, their sorted order may affect behavior; the problem normally uses distinct indices.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(k log k), and repeated slicing/rebuilding can cost O(k*n) time and O(n) temporary space.

Task and constraints: Perform source-to-target replacements at specified indices, using original string positions and matching source text.
Idea: Sort all replacement triples by descending index and apply valid replacements from right to left.
Technique and why it applies: Changes to a later suffix do not shift any earlier original index, so the source slice can be checked directly against the original positions.
Invariant: After processing a replacement at index i, all modifications to its right are complete and do not alter positions before i.
Edge cases: A replacement is skipped if the source does not match. Reverse sorting also defines an order for equal indices, though problem constraints generally avoid conflicting same-index replacements.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(k log k); repeated string slicing and concatenation can take O(k*n) time and O(n) working space.
